# Voyage to the Blue Planet

"Voyage to the Blue Planet" is the title given to a 2024 concert tour headlined by the American rock band Weezer , . The tour was conceived as a large-scale live performance spectacle designed to celebrate the thirtieth anniversary of the band's seminal 1994 self-titled debut album, widely known as *The Blue Album* , , . Unlike a conventional greatest-hits tour, "Voyage to the Blue Planet" was structured around an elaborate, original science-fiction narrative that framed the concerts as a guided storytelling experience rather than a simple collection of songs , . In this conceptual framework, frontman Rivers Cuomo and the band members portrayed astronauts, or "Weezeroids," on a perilous mission to a distant, dying planet to save it by performing the entirety of *The Blue Album* , . The tour's core identity is defined by its fusion of high-concept theatricality, meticulously curated musical selections, and immersive stagecraft, transforming each show into a cohesive, multi-sensory event. It represents a deliberate effort by the band to engage with their legacy in a novel and deeply resonant way, culminating in a full-album performance that served as both a nostalgic homecoming and a powerful artistic statement. The tour ran across North America from September 4, 2024, to October 12, 2024, featuring performances at major arenas and stadiums, and was supported by fellow alternative rock acts The Flaming Lips and Dinosaur Jr. , .

## Tour Concept and Narrative Framework

The foundational concept of "Voyage to the Blue Planet" is its departure from the traditional rock concert format, instead embracing a fully realized, narrative-driven framework that serves as the organizing principle for every aspect of the show . The tour was explicitly launched to commemorate the 30th anniversary of Weezer's 1994 debut album, but its structure transcends a simple chronological celebration, opting instead for a fictionalized journey through space and time , . The central premise, established before the music even begins, casts the band and the audience as a team of alien explorers, dubbed "Weezeroids," tasked with a critical mission , . According to the tour's storyline, these travelers are journeying 30 light-years away to reach a planet designated as the "Blue Planet"—a direct metaphor for Weezer's iconic 1994 album—which is suffering from a severe ecological crisis , . The entire purpose of the voyage is to restore the planet's vitality by performing *The Blue Album* in its entirety, thereby saving it from extinction , . This narrative provides a clear and compelling reason for the concert's structure, turning the act of listening to music into an active, participatory adventure.

The narrative unfolds through a series of scripted interludes delivered by lead singer Rivers Cuomo, synchronized video projections on a massive screen, and carefully choreographed stage effects , . The story begins with the launch of their spacecraft, the "Betsy 2.0," which often involved the band emerging from a giant rocket ship prop or beneath a countdown sequence projected on circular screens , , . Once aboard, the crew embarks on their interstellar journey, depicted through CGI starfield projections, hovering planets, and UFOs that fill the stage and screen, creating a tangible sense of being adrift in the cosmos , . The narrative incorporates a specific antagonist named "Bokkus," described as a character created by drummer Patrick Wilson, adding a layer of conflict to be overcome during the voyage , . A pivotal plot point occurs when the spaceship is forced to crash-land in a region referred to as the "Pinkerton Asteroid Belt" , . This event is not merely a detour but a crucial narrative device that justifies the inclusion of the band's second studio album, *Pinkerton*, within the setlist , . The storyline explains that they must recover essential parts from the wreckage while stranded there, leading directly into the five-song segment dedicated to the *Pinkerton* era , . This integration elevates *Pinkerton*'s status within the band's canon, framing it as a necessary and heroic interlude in their quest.

The climax of the narrative arc involves the successful navigation of the asteroid belt, leading to the final approach and landing on the Blue Planet itself , . During this phase, Cuomo reveals he is an alien from the Blue Planet, a revelation presented as a metaphorical framing device to unify the performance's themes . The planet is symbolically restored upon the completion of the band's mission, often depicted by planting a Weezer flag on a fake rock and releasing blue streamers and confetti , , . Some versions of the story also included a post-credits twist involving a wormhole that alters the timeline, suggesting a playful continuation of the adventure beyond the main performance . This sophisticated narrative structure was praised by critics for its ability to transform a concert into an experience akin to the guided storytelling of Disneyland’s Star Tours combined with the theatrical grandeur of an Iron Maiden show . By providing a clear beginning, middle, and end, the story gave fans a shared mythology to engage with, fostering a deeper connection to the music and the performance itself. The tour's success was heavily dependent on this framework, which provided context and meaning to the song choices, making the evening feel less like a concert and more like a communal myth-making event.

## Musical Architecture and Setlist Structure

The musical architecture of "Voyage to the Blue Planet" is meticulously engineered to mirror the tour's three-part sci-fi narrative, creating a thematic and emotional progression throughout the concert , . The setlist is consistently structured into three distinct segments, each corresponding to a different phase of the fictional voyage . This deliberate sequencing ensures that the performance feels like a cohesive journey rather than a random collection of hits. The first segment, titled "Ascent through the stars," serves to energize the audience and establish the band's broad appeal . It typically opens with a fast-paced medley of career-spanning highlights from various Weezer albums, including tracks like 'Anonymous', 'Hash Pipe', 'Island in the Sun', 'Any Friend of Diane’s', 'Dope Nose', 'Pork and Beans', and 'Beverly Hills' , , , . This opening block is designed to welcome the audience aboard the "Betsy 2.0" and get them singing along immediately, setting a high-energy tone for the evening. For instance, one source notes that the show opened with 'Anonymous' followed by four other songs before transitioning to the next part of the narrative .

The second segment, triggered by the narrative of the spaceship crash in the "Pinkerton Asteroid Belt," features a dedicated block of songs from the band's critically acclaimed but initially commercially underperforming 1996 album, *Pinkerton* , . This section consists of four or five consecutive songs from the album, including tracks like 'Getchoo', 'Why Bother?', 'Pink Triangle', 'Across the Sea', and 'You Gave Your Love to Me Softly' , , . The inclusion of *Pinkerton* is a significant curatorial choice, effectively using the tour's narrative to validate the album's importance within the band's history. By framing the performance of these songs as a necessary action to repair their damaged spacecraft, the tour gives the *Pinkerton* era a heroic and essential role in the overall mission . This strategic placement transforms what could be a jarring tonal shift into a logical and compelling part of the story. The third and most anticipated segment is the culmination of the narrative: a complete, sequential performance of *The Blue Album* , , . This finale includes all ten tracks from the 1994 debut, performed in their original album order [), ]. The set begins with 'My Name Is Jonas' and proceeds through classics like 'In the Garage', 'No One Else', 'Surf Wax America', 'Say It Ain't So', 'In the Garage', and concludes with the epic six-plus-minute closer 'Only in Dreams' , , . Performing the album in its entirety is a major draw for die-hard fans and represents a definitive statement of the band's commitment to their foundational work.

Beyond these three primary segments, the tour also featured deeper cuts and rarities, demonstrating a comprehensive approach to celebrating the band's catalog . These selections underscored the enduring strength of Weezer's songwriting, even when arrangements were adapted for arena-rock scale . The musical choices were strategically balanced to cater to both casual listeners and long-time devotees, ensuring a broad appeal while still delivering a satisfying and deep dive into the band's history. The consistent structure across multiple reported performances—from Boston to Dallas to Philadelphia—indicates that this was a core, intentional design element of the tour, aimed at maximizing both fan engagement and narrative coherence , , . The careful sequencing ensured that the emotional weight of the performance built steadily, peaking with the cathartic and unifying experience of hearing *The Blue Album* played from start to finish in a live setting.

## Production Design and Audience Engagement

The production design of "Voyage to the Blue Planet" was integral to the tour's success, creating an immersive environment that brought the sci-fi narrative to life and fostered a strong sense of community among the audience , . The staging and visual elements were meticulously crafted to transport concertgoers to another world, functioning as a "fifth band member" that interacted with the music and story in real time . Key components of the stagecraft included NASA-style astronaut jumpsuits worn by the band members, reinforcing the "Weezeroids" concept and creating a unified visual identity , . The centerpiece of the stage often involved a giant foam space capsule or a rocket ship prop that would emerge from the floor or launch into the rafters, serving as the focal point for the show's opening moments , . Other physical props included fog machines, sparks, and space boulders on stage, further enhancing the tangible sense of being on a space mission , . The color palette was dominated by blues and purples, with blue-lit seats, flying blue streamers, and flashing blue lights creating a cohesive and atmospheric soundscape .

A defining feature of the production was the extensive use of synchronized CGI visuals projected onto a massive screen behind the band , . These animations acted as a dynamic backdrop, illustrating the narrative beats of the show. For example, during the "Ascent through the stars," audiences saw animated backdrops of galaxies and interplanetary travel , . The visuals were intricately linked to the music; one report noted that the song 'Island in the Sun' was depicted onscreen as an island floating inside a sun, adding a layer of creative interpretation to the performance . The screen also displayed images of "skinny, bespectacled space travelers" modeled after Rivers Cuomo, further blurring the line between the performers and their fictional personas . This multimedia approach ensured that every moment of the concert felt like a scene from a larger story, rewarding attentive viewers with a richly detailed world to explore.

This elaborate production design successfully cultivated a highly engaged and emotionally resonant audience experience. Eyewitness accounts and reviews describe a crowd that was not merely passive but actively participated in the shared fantasy , . Fans sang every word of the songs, swayed in unison during melodic passages, and erupted in cheers during climactic moments . Specific call-and-response moments became highlights, such as the collective scream of "hip, hip" during 'Island in the Sun' or the audience taking over the chorus of 'Undone — The Sweater Song' during a deliberate band silence . The tour also fostered a powerful sense of intergenerational connection, with reports of middle-aged fans attending with their children and parents reliving their own youth through shared nostalgia , . The emotional core of the show was palpable, particularly during the performance of 'Say It Ain’t So', which was described as having a "ferocious" and cathartic impact on the audience , and the closing track 'Only in Dreams', where a mosh pit reportedly broke out—the first time frontman Rivers Cuomo had witnessed such a reaction to that song live . This deep level of engagement suggests that the combination of the narrative framework, high-quality production, and well-chosen music successfully tapped into a collective cultural memory, making the experience feel uniquely personal and profoundly impactful for attendees.

## Critical Reception and Cultural Resonance

The critical reception for "Voyage to the Blue Planet" was overwhelmingly positive, with reviewers praising the tour's innovative blend of narrative storytelling, theatrical production, and authentic rock & roll energy . The consensus opinion framed the concert not merely as a retrospective but as a new form of live entertainment that redefined the possibilities of a modern rock show. A prominent review from *Rolling Stone* captured this sentiment perfectly, describing the experience as "the meeting point between the guided narrative of Disneyland’s Star Tours and the rock & roll theatrics of an Iron Maiden show" and concluding that "this is the Weezer arena show we want" . This comparison highlights the tour's unique achievement in balancing the polished, story-driven spectacle of a theme park ride with the raw, visceral power of a metal concert. The praise extended to the emotional depth of the performance, with outlets like *Variety* noting that the show evoked "countless memories listening to Weezer" and highlighted its ability to resonate emotionally across the band's entire discography . Critics lauded the seamless integration of the sci-fi narrative with the setlist, calling it a culturally resonant event that was "orbit-defining" in its impact . The production itself was frequently described as ambitious and effective, with one review comparing the elaborate staging to "Disney World run amok," suggesting a sense of wonder and awe that elevated the experience beyond a standard gig .

Beyond the initial critical acclaim, the tour demonstrated significant cultural resonance, tapping into a deep vein of nostalgia among Weezer's long-standing fanbase while also introducing the band's legacy to a new generation , . The decision to perform *The Blue Album* in its entirety was a powerful gesture that affirmed the album's status as a cornerstone of 1990s alternative rock [), ]. The tour's narrative provided a fresh and compelling lens through which to view the band's history, particularly by giving the *Pinkerton* album a prominent and heroic role , . This curatorial choice was seen as a bold and intelligent move that validated the album's artistic merit and solidified its place in the band's official canon. The enthusiastic audience response, characterized by singalongs, synchronized drumming, and visible emotional catharsis, confirmed the tour's success in forging a strong communal bond among attendees . Reports of sold-out shows at major venues, such as two nights at The Anthem in Washington, D.C., which grossed $816,250 per show, indicated strong commercial viability alongside its artistic success .

The tour's impact extends beyond the immediate concert experience. It represented a masterful piece of marketing and commemoration, timed perfectly to capitalize on the 30th anniversary of *The Blue Album* , . The release of a comprehensive 3CD/4LP box set on November 1, 2024, containing 40 bonus tracks—including unreleased demos and BBC recordings—was a coordinated effort to deepen the celebration and provide lasting value for collectors , , . This synergy between the live tour and ancillary releases created a multifaceted cultural moment centered on Weezer's legacy. The tour's emphasis on nostalgia was not simply a look backward but a reaffirmation of the band's enduring relevance and the timeless quality of their music. By embedding their songs within a compelling fictional narrative, Weezer successfully transformed a series of concerts into a shared cultural event, leaving a lasting impression on both critics and fans alike.

## Tour Logistics and Ancillary Releases

The "Voyage to the Blue Planet" tour was a major North American concert tour undertaken by Weezer in 2024, comprising a single leg with 22 to 24 officially confirmed performances , . The tour commenced on September 4, 2024, at the Xcel Energy Center in Saint Paul, Minnesota, and concluded on October 12, 2024, at Acrisure Arena in Palm Desert, California , , . The dates spanned several weeks, allowing the band to visit numerous cities across the United States and Canada. The tour's logistical details reflect a large-scale production, with performances held in some of the country's largest and most prominent venues, including Madison Square Garden in New York City, TD Garden in Boston, Wells Fargo Center in Philadelphia, Moody Center in Austin, Toyota Center in Houston, and Intuit Dome in Los Angeles , , , , . Support for the tour was provided by two influential alternative rock bands, The Flaming Lips and Dinosaur Jr., whose distinct styles complemented Weezer's sound and the tour's nostalgic, experimental ethos , , . Dinosaur Jr. contributed their signature alt-rock sound characterized by heavy guitar distortion and a DIY ethos, while The Flaming Lips offered a psychedelic rock set featuring elaborate stage props and intimate crowd interaction , . The presence of these acts helped create a cohesive and thematically rich concert experience for attendees.

A significant ancillary release accompanying the tour was the concert film, *Weezer's Voyage to the Blue Planet: The Concert Film*. This film was shot during the band's performance at TD Garden in Boston, Massachusetts on September 10, 2024, capturing a night of the tour that received widespread critical attention [), , ]. The film was made available to the public through a livestream exclusively on the platform Moment.co, with screenings scheduled for October 13 and 14, 2024 , . Tickets for the livestream were priced at $13 for early-bird purchases and increased to $16 or $18 depending on availability, with a 24-hour replay option offered after each screening . This digital release strategy allowed fans who were unable to attend the live shows to experience the tour's theatrical spectacle. Beyond the film, the tour was part of a larger commemorative campaign centered on the 30th anniversary of *The Blue Album*. On November 1, 2024, UMe (Geffen/UMe) released the *Blue Album 30th Anniversary Super Deluxe Edition* , , . This expansive package contained 50 previously unreleased tracks across four 12-inch LPs, a 10-inch EP, and a 7-inch record, offering fans unprecedented access to the band's early development . The release included a wealth of archival material, such as the 1992 'Kitchen Tape' demos, early rehearsal takes from Loyola Marymount University, live recordings from LA clubs, and rare BBC radio sessions , , . The physical packaging was designed with collectible items, including lithographs, stickers, a poster, and an enamel pin shaped like the antagonist Bokkus, further enhancing its value for dedicated fans , .

## Legacy and Commemorative Significance

The "Voyage to the Blue Planet" tour holds significant commemorative and historical importance within Weezer's career and the landscape of modern rock tours. Its primary legacy is its role as a landmark celebration of the 30th anniversary of *The Blue Album*, an album that is widely regarded as one of the defining works of the 1990s alternative rock movement , . The tour was far more than a mere re-release of the album's songs; it was a thoughtful and ambitious reinterpretation that placed the music within a new, imaginative context. By embedding the performance of *The Blue Album* into a cohesive science-fiction narrative, Weezer elevated the album from a static collection of songs to a living, breathing mythology , . This approach demonstrated a profound respect for the material and a desire to share its magic with fans in a way that felt both reverent and excitingly new. The tour's success in achieving this balance has likely influenced how the band approaches its own legacy and how other artists might frame their own anniversary celebrations.

Furthermore, the tour's structure and narrative logic provided a powerful and unexpected validation for the band's often-maligned 1996 album, *Pinkerton*. Historically, *Pinkerton* was viewed as a commercial failure and a stylistic departure from the polished pop sensibilities of *The Blue Album* . However, by framing the *Pinkerton* segment as a crucial and heroic detour—a necessary stop to fix their spaceship—the tour reframed the album as an essential chapter in the band's story , . This narrative justification gave the album a newfound prominence and has likely contributed to a re-evaluation of its artistic worth among both critics and fans. The tour effectively argued that *Pinkerton* was not a step backward but a vital part of the band's journey, enriching the overall narrative of their career. This curatorial decision showcased a mature understanding of the band's entire discography and demonstrated a willingness to champion all facets of their creative output.

In conclusion, the "Voyage to the Blue Planet" tour's legacy is that of a creatively ambitious and commercially successful commemorative event that successfully blended nostalgia with innovation. It proved that a full-album tour could be more than a simple greatest-hits set by weaving the music into a compelling story. The tour's emphasis on narrative, its meticulous production design, and its deep engagement with its fanbase set a new standard for how classic rock catalogs can be presented live. Its impact will likely be felt in the years to come, not only as a cherished memory for those who attended but also as a case study in how to honor a musical legacy with imagination, integrity, and theatrical flair. The tour stands as a testament to the enduring power of Weezer's music and the band's continued ability to connect with their audience through creative and meaningful artistic expression.

These animations acted as a dynamic backdrop, illustrating the narrative beats of the show.
During the "Ascent through the stars," audiences saw animated backdrops of galaxies and interplanetary travel.
The visuals were intricately linked to the music.
One report noted that the song 'Island in the Sun' was depicted onscreen as an island floating inside a sun, adding a layer of creative interpretation to the performance.
The screen also displayed images of "skinny, bespectacled space travelers" modeled after Rivers Cuomo.
This multimedia approach ensured that every moment of the concert felt like a scene from a larger story.
The multimedia approach rewarded attentive viewers with a richly detailed world to explore.
This elaborate production design successfully cultivated a highly engaged and emotionally resonant audience experience.
Eyewitness accounts and reviews describe a crowd that was not merely passive but actively participated in the shared fantasy.
Fans sang every word of the songs, swayed in unison during melodic passages, and erupted in cheers during climactic moments.
Specific call-and-response moments became highlights, such as the collective scream of "hip, hip" during 'Island in the Sun'.
The audience taking over the chorus of 'Undone — The Sweater Song' during a deliberate band silence was a highlight.
The tour also fostered a powerful sense of intergenerational connection.
Reports exist of middle-aged fans attending with their children and parents reliving their own youth through shared nostalgia.
The emotional core of the show was palpable, particularly during the performance of 'Say It Ain’t So'.
'Say It Ain’t So' was described as having a "ferocious" and cathartic impact on the audience.
During the closing track 'Only in Dreams', a mosh pit reportedly broke out.
This was the first time frontman Rivers Cuomo had witnessed such a reaction to 'Only in Dreams' live.
This deep level of engagement suggests that the combination of the narrative framework, high-quality production, and well-chosen music successfully tapped into a collective cultural memory.
The combination made the experience feel uniquely personal and profoundly impactful for attendees.
The critical reception for "Voyage to the Blue Planet" was overwhelmingly positive.
Reviewers praised the tour's innovative blend of narrative storytelling, theatrical production, and authentic rock & roll energy.
The consensus opinion framed the concert not merely as a retrospective but as a new form of live entertainment.
The concert redefined the possibilities of a modern rock show.
A prominent review from *Rolling Stone* described the experience as "the meeting point between the guided narrative of Disneyland’s Star Tours and the rock & roll theatrics of an Iron Maiden show."
*Rolling Stone* concluded that "this is the Weezer arena show we want."
This comparison highlights the tour's unique achievement in balancing the polished, story-driven spectacle of a theme park ride with the raw, visceral power of a metal concert.
The praise extended to the emotional depth of the performance.
Outlets like *Variety* noted that the show evoked "countless memories listening to Weezer."
*Variety* highlighted the show's ability to resonate emotionally across the band's entire discography.
Critics lauded the seamless integration of the sci-fi narrative with the setlist.
The integration was called a culturally resonant event that was "orbit-defining" in its impact.
The production itself was frequently described as ambitious and effective.
One review compared the elaborate staging to "Disney World run amok."
The comparison suggested a sense of wonder and awe that elevated the experience beyond a standard gig.
Beyond the initial critical acclaim, the tour demonstrated significant cultural resonance.
The tour tapped into a deep vein of nostalgia among Weezer's long-standing fanbase.
The tour introduced the band's legacy to a new generation.
The decision to perform *The Blue Album* in its entirety was a powerful gesture.
The gesture affirmed *The Blue Album*'s status as a cornerstone of 1990s alternative rock.
The tour's narrative provided a fresh and compelling lens through which to view the band's history.
The narrative gave the *Pinkerton* album a prominent and heroic role.
This curatorial choice was seen as a bold and intelligent move.
The move validated *Pinkerton*'s artistic merit and solidified its place in the band's official canon.
The enthusiastic audience response, characterized by singalongs, synchronized drumming, and visible emotional catharsis, confirmed the tour's success.
The tour succeeded in forging a strong communal bond among attendees.
Reports of sold-out shows at major venues, such as two nights at The Anthem in Washington, D.C., indicated strong commercial viability alongside its artistic success.
The two nights at The Anthem in Washington, D.C., grossed $816,250 per show.
The tour's impact extends beyond the immediate concert experience.
It represented a masterful piece of marketing and commemoration, timed perfectly to capitalize on the 30th anniversary of *The Blue Album*.

The release of a comprehensive 3CD/4LP box set on November 1, 2024, containing 40 bonus tracks—including unreleased demos and BBC recordings—was a coordinated effort to deepen the celebration and provide lasting value for collectors.
This synergy between the live tour and ancillary releases created a multifaceted cultural moment centered on Weezer's legacy.
The tour's emphasis on nostalgia was not simply a look backward but a reaffirmation of the band's enduring relevance.
The tour's emphasis on nostalgia was a reaffirmation of the timeless quality of their music.
By embedding their songs within a compelling fictional narrative, Weezer successfully transformed a series of concerts into a shared cultural event.
The transformation left a lasting impression on both critics and fans alike.
The "Voyage to the Blue Planet" tour was a major North American concert tour undertaken by Weezer in 2024.
The tour comprised a single leg with 22 to 24 officially confirmed performances.
The tour commenced on September 4, 2024, at the Xcel Energy Center in Saint Paul, Minnesota.
The tour concluded on October 12, 2024, at Acrisure Arena in Palm Desert, California.
The dates spanned several weeks, allowing the band to visit numerous cities across the United States and Canada.
The tour's logistical details reflect a large-scale production.

Performances were held in some of the country's largest and most prominent venues, including Madison Square Garden in New York City, TD Garden in Boston, Wells Fargo Center in Philadelphia, Moody Center in Austin, Toyota Center in Houston, and Intuit Dome in Los Angeles.
Support for the tour was provided by two influential alternative rock bands, The Flaming Lips and Dinosaur Jr.
Their distinct styles complemented Weezer's sound and the tour's nostalgic, experimental ethos.
Dinosaur Jr. contributed their signature alt-rock sound characterized by heavy guitar distortion and a DIY ethos.
The Flaming Lips offered a psychedelic rock set featuring elaborate stage props and intimate crowd interaction.
The presence of these acts helped create a cohesive and thematically rich concert experience for attendees.
A significant ancillary release accompanying the tour was the concert film, *Weezer's Voyage to the Blue Planet: The Concert Film*.
This film was shot during the band's performance at TD Garden in Boston, Massachusetts on September 10, 2024.
The film captured a night of the tour that received widespread critical attention.
The film was made available to the public through a livestream exclusively on the platform Moment.co.
Screenings were scheduled for October 13 and 14, 2024.
Tickets for the livestream were priced at $13 for early-bird purchases.
Tickets increased to $16 or $18 depending on availability.
A 24-hour replay option was offered after each screening.
This digital release strategy allowed fans who were unable to attend the live shows to experience the tour's theatrical spectacle.
Beyond the film, the tour was part of a larger commemorative campaign centered on the 30th anniversary of *The Blue Album*.
On November 1, 2024, UMe (Geffen/UMe) released the *Blue Album 30th Anniversary Super Deluxe Edition*.
This expansive package contained 50 previously unreleased tracks across four 12-inch LPs, a 10-inch EP, and a 7-inch record.
The package offered fans unprecedented access to the band's early development.

The release included a wealth of archival material, such as the 1992 'Kitchen Tape' demos, early rehearsal takes from Loyola Marymount University, live recordings from LA clubs, and rare BBC radio sessions.
The physical packaging was designed with collectible items, including lithographs, stickers, a poster, and an enamel pin shaped like the antagonist Bokkus.
The packaging further enhanced its value for dedicated fans.
The "Voyage to the Blue Planet" Tour Launch was on September 4, 2024, at Xcel Energy Center, St. Paul, MN.
The Tour Launch was the official start of the North American tour.
The Concert Film Recording for *Weezer's Voyage to the Blue Planet: The Concert Film* was on September 10, 2024, at TD Garden, Boston, MA.
The performance at TD Garden was filmed for subsequent livestream release.
A Major Venue Show for the "Voyage to the Blue Planet" Tour was on September 11, 2024, at Madison Square Garden, NY, NY.
The Madison Square Garden show included support from The Flaming Lips and Dinosaur Jr.
International Dates for the "Voyage to the Blue Planet" Tour are January 5–8, 2025, in Chiba, Osaka, Nagoya, Japan.
An international leg of the tour was announced for early 2025.
The Concert Film Release for *Weezer's Voyage to the Blue Planet: The Concert Film* was on October 13–14, 2024, via Livestream on Moment.co.
The Concert Film Release consisted of exclusive online screenings of the Boston performance.
The Box Set Release for *Blue Album 30th Anniversary Super Deluxe Edition* was on November 1, 2024, globally.
The Box Set includes 50 unreleased tracks and physical extras.
The "Voyage to the Blue Planet" tour holds significant commemorative and historical importance within Weezer's career.
The tour holds significant commemorative and historical importance within the landscape of modern rock tours.
Its primary legacy is its role as a landmark celebration of the 30th anniversary of *The Blue Album*.
*The Blue Album* is widely regarded as one of the defining works of the 1990s alternative rock movement.
The tour was far more than a mere re-release of the album's songs.
The tour was a thoughtful and ambitious reinterpretation that placed the music within a new, imaginative context.
By embedding the performance of *The Blue Album* into a cohesive science-fiction narrative, Weezer elevated the album from a static collection of songs to a living, breathing mythology.
This approach demonstrated a profound respect for the material.
This approach demonstrated a desire to share its magic with fans in a way that felt both reverent and excitingly new.
The tour's success in achieving this balance has likely influenced how the band approaches its own legacy.
The tour's success has likely influenced how other artists might frame their own anniversary celebrations.
Furthermore, the tour's structure and narrative logic provided a powerful and unexpected validation for the band's often-maligned 1996 album, *Pinkerton*.
Historically, *Pinkerton* was viewed as a commercial failure.
*Pinkerton* was viewed as a stylistic departure from the polished pop sensibilities of *The Blue Album*.
By framing the *Pinkerton* segment as a crucial and heroic detour—a necessary stop to fix their spaceship—the tour reframed the album as an essential chapter in the band's story.
This narrative justification gave the album a newfound prominence.
This narrative justification has likely contributed to a re-evaluation of its artistic worth among both critics and fans.
The tour effectively argued that *Pinkerton* was not a step backward but a vital part of the band's journey.
The tour enriched the overall narrative of their career.
This curatorial decision showcased a mature understanding of the band's entire discography.
This curatorial decision demonstrated a willingness to champion all facets of their creative output.
The "Voyage to the Blue Planet" tour's legacy is that of a creatively ambitious and commercially successful commemorative event.
The tour successfully blended nostalgia with innovation.
It proved that a full-album tour could be more than a simple greatest-hits set by weaving the music into a compelling story.
The tour's emphasis on narrative, its meticulous production design, and its deep engagement with its fanbase set a new standard for how classic rock catalogs can be presented live.

Its impact will likely be felt in the years to come, not only as a cherished memory for those who attended but also as a case study in how to honor a musical legacy with imagination, integrity, and theatrical flair.
The tour stands as a testament to the enduring power of Weezer's music.
The tour stands as a testament to the band's continued ability to connect with their audience through creative and meaningful artistic expression.

MUSIC REVIEW

Weezer takes fans on a space-age voyage with rockin’ TD Garden show
===================================================================

[](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2024/09/11/arts/weezer-boston-concert-review-td-garden/#bgmp-comments)

![Image 8: Singer and guitarist Rivers Cuomo performed with Weezer at TD Garden on Tuesday.](https://bostonglobe-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/resizer/v2/VGF6GO5XCX7ULTR4PYUPC5PHQE.jpg?auth=ce54316186334bb9d15aa58250a90e94642dc0d16109951698496759481b8a8b&width=1440)

Singer and guitarist Rivers Cuomo performed with Weezer at TD Garden on Tuesday.Ben Stas for The Boston Globe

The planet is dying, and only a celebration of a 30-year-old, tongue-in-cheek pop-rock album can save it. That’s the premise behind Weezer’s elaborate “Voyage to the Blue Planet” tour, which set up shop at TD Garden on Tuesday.

For a famously eggheaded band that has always looked askance at the self-seriousness of rock ‘n’ roll cliches, the over-the-top space-age staging was an amusing joke that maybe extended itself a bit far.

![Image 9: Weezer performed at TD Garden on Tuesday.](https://bostonglobe-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/resizer/v2/TEBXGT37DG3KKUCS3JP6E4ZCFE.jpg?auth=0fcc8cea977732f73bb17ac8fbab9a1e0b0b7b3acace418dd190e849e8ff9db5&width=1440)

Weezer performed at TD Garden on Tuesday.Ben Stas for The Boston Globe/The Boston Globe

Weezer’s self-titled debut, universally known as “The Blue Album,” was an anomaly in 1994 — a bit grungy, yes, but also unabashedly informed by classic power-pop bands and melodic vocals. The Cars’s Ric Ocasek produced the album.

On Tuesday, when the massive screen behind the band flashed an animated video featuring a battalion of skinny, bespectacled space travelers — clones of Rivers Cuomo, Weezer’s conspicuous frontman — guitarist Brian Bell feigned ignorance about who they were.

FEATURED VIDEO

* * *

* * *

“Oh, those are Weezeroids,” Cuomo replied, sticking to the script.

The band’s New England-area Weezeroids, mostly middle-aged, some younger, nearly filled the Garden. As advertised, Weezer played all of the Blue Album (including the big MTV hits “Buddy Holly,” “Undone — The Sweater Song,” and “Say It Ain’t So”) in its entirety. Prior to that, they unspooled a tight, fast-paced set of career highlights (“Beverly Hills,” “Island in the Sun,” “Hash Pipe”) and a five-song nod to “Pinkerton,” the band’s polarizing second album.

“Hello! Welcome to the Very Good Show!” Dinosaur Jr. bassist Lou Barlow announced when the long-running noise band from Amherst occupied a tiny portion of the stage as the opening act. From the moment that guitarist [J Mascis](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2024/01/29/arts/j-mascis-dinosaur-jr-food-amherst/) plugged in, the arena filled with crackling, ear-splitting feedback. The band played a half-dozen of their most notable songs, including “Feel the Pain,” “Freak Scene,” and their arch cover of the Cure’s “Just Like Heaven.”

Advertisement

* * *

* * *

![Image 10: Singer and guitarist J Mascis performs with Dinosaur Jr. at TD Garden on Tuesday.](https://bostonglobe-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/resizer/v2/PIOAA5EYISAZYECTY323BSX3JU.jpg?auth=4a58fd39c2c5e25264d4bcdb730408e25d9ed2a2de3c5df2559f71d28136b7e2&width=1440)

Singer and guitarist J Mascis performs with Dinosaur Jr. at TD Garden on Tuesday.Ben Stas for The Boston Globe/The Boston Globe

The pop-psychedelic Flaming Lips held up their end of the burlesque bargain. The band’s hourlong set featured the usual array of inflatable shenanigans — dancing eyeballs, two huge pink robots, a “magic” rainbow. At one point the rat’s-nest-coiffed frontman Wayne Coyne put on a Wonder Woman robe.

Earlier, Coyne pulled out a piece of paper and read from a long list of Boston-area venues the band has played over its 40-year history, including Molly’s, [the Rat](https://www.bostonglobe.com/magazine/2017/06/06/closed-years-ago-but-rat-rollicking-echoes-reverb/Y4Zf8mlZ83mQ65veK1JB3O/story.html), Green Street Station, and [TT the Bear’s Place](https://www.bostonglobe.com/arts/music/2015/07/16/after-years-cambridge-legendary-club-bear-place-calls-night/tw4iusGlhMTWVobUGo7laK/story.html).

![Image 11: Singer Wayne Coyne performed with The Flaming Lips at TD Garden on Tuesday.](https://bostonglobe-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/resizer/v2/GOHPS7CBU7ETR7TRJQV43AAQ4M.jpg?auth=472ae44b212d897d5ebcba91e3258c0af4df89db2d60a7fcb355c737a3f783e9&width=1440)

Singer Wayne Coyne performed with The Flaming Lips at TD Garden on Tuesday.Ben Stas for The Boston Globe/The Boston Globe

Like the opening act, the Lips goofed on the ‘80s, covering Madonna’s “Borderline.” “Feels like I’m going to lose my mind,” Coyne warbled, aptly, given his band’s long-term commitment to weirdness for its own sake.

Weezer’s brand of weirdness is far more deadpan, an attribute that helped sell the gimmick of its extravagant stage design. After a fake “breaking news” segment aired about the impending voyage, a five-minute countdown led to a giant foam space capsule at center stage achieving liftoff. Like a latter-day Devo, the four members of the band came out in matching jumpsuits.

![Image 12: Guitarist Brian Bell, left and singer and guitarist Rivers Cuomo performed with Weezer at TD Garden on Tuseday.](https://bostonglobe-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/resizer/v2/V4D3DR6HMPM7DSJA2XF7IG23DY.jpg?auth=1733177f6f4993dd091d44b6286c2770e79176eef40c35058a2d6376d69a125f&width=1440)

Guitarist Brian Bell, left and singer and guitarist Rivers Cuomo performed with Weezer at TD Garden on Tuseday.Ben Stas for The Boston Globe/The Boston Globe

“Thanks for coming on this very dangerous, very important mission!” said the poker-faced Cuomo. Having grown up a fan of heavy metal guitar shredders, he can play wrenching, ringing solos, but he does so with the demeanor of a guy waiting in line at the RMV.

“Scanning for civilization,” intoned an Alexa-like voice before the “Blue Album” showcase began. “Searching for signs of life.” By then, the kitschy video-game backdrop had worn a little thin, but the band soldiered along.

![Image 13: Bassist Scott Shriner performed with Weezer at TD Garden on Tuseday.](https://bostonglobe-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/resizer/v2/RTUBSYVBYNHZZ2QDN4AJ6IVZOE.jpg?auth=dbd8baf9d339b0c279cad3225eee6ff7f821d2c3cdd2cae2158201d596f23c22&width=1440)

Bassist Scott Shriner performed with Weezer at TD Garden on Tuseday.Ben Stas for The Boston Globe/The Boston Globe

No pandering was necessary to get the crowd in the mood for those final 10 songs (though Bell did drop a reference to clam chowder into his spoken intro to “The Sweater Song”). With the band’s guitars and voices meshing, more than once Cuomo and bassist Scott Shriner both put a foot up on their monitors to rock out. In the moment, those poses felt genuine.

Advertisement

* * *

* * *

And when the band arrived at the album’s last cut, the slow-burning, eight-minute power ballad “Only in Dreams,” a mosh pit broke out on the Garden floor. It was, Cuomo said, the first time he’d seen that happen.

“We made it, guys,” he told the crowd. “Thirty light years.”

![Image 14: Weezer performed at TD Garden on Tuesday.](https://bostonglobe-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/resizer/v2/EA6F4PTHEOKLFHH6LXHMPBSXPM.jpg?auth=68e1c37550c8b6daf1b6d73a9cdf30ddc36b9fa54fd1a01657903a14e78a9eaa&width=1440)

Weezer performed at TD Garden on Tuesday.Ben Stas for The Boston Globe/The Boston Globe

**WEEZER: VOYAGE TO THE BLUE PLANET TOUR**

With Dinosaur Jr. and the Flaming Lips

At TD Garden, Tuesday

Review | Weezer’s Voyage to the Blue Planet
===========================================

The Band Celebrates 30 Years of Their Iconic ‘Blue Album’

 ![Image 2: Author Image](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/9a779c59aa65a254850ddf36f21928c454d87007f418b6865ce755e928ecb526?s=50&d=mm&r=g)By [Kat Sophia](https://www.independent.com/author/kaatshengmail-com/ "Posts by Kat Sophia")  
Wed Oct 16, 2024 | 10:56am

### Share this:

*   [Click to share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook](https://www.independent.com/2024/10/16/review-weezers-voyage-to-the-blue-planet/?share=facebook)
*   [Click to share on X (Opens in new window) X](https://www.independent.com/2024/10/16/review-weezers-voyage-to-the-blue-planet/?share=x)

[Add independent.com on Google Add the SB Independent as your preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=independent.com)

![Image 3](https://www.independent.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/weezer-Brendan-Walter.jpeg)

Weezer | Photo: Brendan Walter

“Beverly Hills, that’s where I want to be … rollin’ like a celebrity.”

Whenever Weezer’s “Beverly Hills” came on the radio when I was a kid, I would air guitar and drum in the backseat of the car as though my life depended on it. The way the band’s songs were recorded, it was hard not to. The brash, loud sounds of the live sounding instrumentation, the tastefully simple melodies, and their conversational lyrics were perfect sonic fodder for a little burgeoning music nerd. Through the airwaves, Weezer became a huge part of my childhood and love of bands. Their music dominated the ’90s with platinum records and chart success, with their rock/emo-meets-pop sound.

Not too far from The Hills themselves, I went to see Weezer at the new Intuit Dome in Inglewood this past week. Celebrating 30 years of the band’s iconic self-titled LP (a k a _The Blue Album_) on their _The Voyage to the Blue Planet_ tour, they created a show where (dressed as astronauts) they are on a mission throughout the set list to play _The Blue Album_ in full.

The show started with the stage set up with a rocket ship in the center, along with a giant screen behind them displaying space imagery. There was a countdown on the side screens, and once it hit zero, the ship lifted to show the band underneath. The band exploded into “Anonymous” as the crowd roared. They played a string of hits, including “Pork and Beans,” “Island in the Sun,” and “Beverly Hills.” During “Island in the Sun,” the audience screamed “hip, hip” along with the band, and during “Beverly Hills,” the lead singer and guitarist swayed in unison back and forth, beaming as they played in tandem with one another.

The band then played a string of cuts from their album _Pinkerton_ as they entered the Pinkerton Asteroid Belt, with highlights including “Pink Triangle,” “Across the Sea,” and “Why Bother?” After “Across the Sea,” the band then grabbed a blue flag and stuck it into the stage, announcing that they had found their way to the Blue Planet.

Weezer played the entire _Blue Album_ top to bottom, and the audience loved it. Most people around me knew every word, and each song was filled with raucous, joyous energy as audience members jumped with joy and clutched each other’s hands as they sang the words to each other, laughing. And there was blue everywhere: Streamers flew through the air, the seats all lit up blue, and the blue lights flashed across the venue. During fan favorite “Say It Ain’t So,” the band looked the most excited of the night, genuinely enjoying watching audience members scream along.

After “Buddy Holly,” lead singer Rivers Cuomo punched both fists into the air in excitement. And during “Undone — The Sweater Song,” the band dropped silent during the chorus, letting the audience take over. It elicited a huge response from the crowd, as fans beamed while singing, “If you want to destroy my sweater, hold this thread as I walk away. Watch me unravel, I’ll soon be naked, lying on the floor.”

Toward the end of the show, I turned around to see an ocean of middle-aged men mimicking the same drum solos I did as a kid. A united community of fans in their own private worlds, it was a celebration together of the music that we’ve explored inside ourselves; embodying each band member as if you were part of the group. I wondered how many other people were tapping into that same kid. It was a blast being her again for a night.

Concert Review: Weezer / Flaming Lips (Columbus, OH)
====================================================

![Image 16: Matt Gallant](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/838cfb073130dbc06a75e40f2420643ca970cdefcd151c2846dde6bc65f1f2f2?s=80&d=mm&r=g) by [Matt Gallant](https://cleverock.com/author/m_gallant/)

[September 8, 2024](https://cleverock.com/concert-review-weezer-flaming-lips-columbus-oh/)

in [Concert Reviews](https://cleverock.com/category/concert-reviews/)

Reading Time: 4 mins read

[![Image 17](https://cleverock-s3-bucket.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/2024/09/Weezer-9-1140x1168.jpg)](https://cleverock-s3-bucket.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/2024/09/Weezer-9.jpg)

Weezer took a sold-out Nationwide Arena on a Voyage to the Blue Planet Saturday night (09.07.24). Their eponymous debut, known colloquially as the Blue Album, was released 30 years ago, and **Rivers Cuomo** and company are currently on tour playing the record in its entirety. The “voyage” to get there was a setlist of one or two songs each from seven or so of their albums, followed by five songs from **‘Pinkerton,’** and, finally, the entire blue album.

The big takeaway of the evening was that the blue album holds up as one of the best rock albums ever. That’s not hyperbole (at least not for me). It’s such a solid, tight collection of 10 songs, front to back. Not a minute of fluff. I’ve been to a few of these album-in-their-entirety-style shows now, and there are usually some slow moments; not so with the blue album! From the opening guitar riff on _“My Name is Jonas”_ to the final bass notes on _“Only in Dreams,”_ it’s such a strong album. Hearing those songs live solidifies its greatness.

I don’t need to go on about the album itself. If you haven’t listened to it, do. But I recommend seeing them live. Even the stage production was next level. It felt like something you’d see on Broadway. The conceit of the show was a literal voyage through space, which played on a screen behind them, in order to get to the Blue Planet. It kicked off with the band emerging from a rocket ship after the top lifted off of the stage and allowed them to come out. There were spaced-themed props, and the band interacted with what was happening behind them. There was a stop at **Pinkerton** asteroid belt, which preceded the five songs off that album. There was a crash landing where Cuomo talked to the sentient spaceship on the screen. There was a moment when Rivers revealed that he as an alien from the Blue Planet, and there were many Weezeroids that looked just like him there.

\[VIDEO COURTESY OF YOUTUBE USER [Theresa Hacker](https://www.youtube.com/@TheresaHacker)}

If all that sounds complicated and a bit unnecessary, maybe, but what kept it fun was that the band wasn’t taking the whole thing too seriously. They knew it was silly and let everyone in on the silliness. Before the rocket launch, there was a pre-launch “interview” over the speaker system with the members about their upcoming mission and how each member was preparing for the voyage. They let it be known that the situation was ridiculous. But it was a great example of how Weezer, and Cuomo specifically, have always been able to walk the tightrope of brooding introverts and nonchalant goofballs.

Before **Dinosaur Jr** played, someone told me that after going to thousands of shows over the years, Dinosaur Jr was the loudest band they had ever seen, which had me looking forward to them as the opener. However, since they only had a six-song set, and were the first of two openers, they didn’t have the chance to showcase their full punk-roots noise onslaught. It was still a great set of straightforward crowd-pleasers, but I would have liked to have seen them get really crazy. The band was able to showcase their ability as extremely talented musicians in that brief time. Watching the bassist, **Lou Barlow**, play his instrument like he is on lead guitar is really something else, and **Murph** is such a specifically great drummer. **J Mascis** did his standard, slacker/genius performance on songs like _“Feel the Pain,”_ and _“Freak Scene,”_ and I loved every bit of it. No, they weren’t as loud as I expected, but they still rocked.

Weezer, however was loud! When standing near the front, it felt like my organs were getting rearranged.

The night was full of hits, from all three bands. The Flaming Lips, among other songs, played _“Yoshimi Battles the Pink Robots,” “She Don’t Use Jelly,” “Do You Realize??,”_ and even a cover of Madonna’s _“Borderline.”_ They had a particularly touching moment when lead singer **Wayne Coyne** pulled out a piece of paper and read a dedication to a song to a young boy whose mother had died in a car accident. They were only able to get in ten songs as the opener, but they still brought their big stage production with them. They had the large inflatable pink robots and the “Fuck Yeah, Columbus,” balloon they bring to every city. The efficiency of it all was impressive.

That was another accidental theme of the night. Everything was so good, you wanted more of it all. That’s the only problem with the blue album: it’s just too short. Weezer, of course, made up for that by the first two parts of the show, but I could have just watched them play the blue album a couple of times in a row. It’s just that fun to see it live.

[![Image 18: Weezer Setlist Nationwide Arena, Columbus, OH, USA 2024, The Voyage to the Blue Planet Tour](https://www.setlist.fm/widgets/setlist-image-v1?id=63aba2ef)](https://www.setlist.fm/setlist/weezer/2024/nationwide-arena-columbus-oh-63aba2ef.html)

[![Image 1: Weezer on Xcel Center stage.](https://themacweekly.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Screenshot-2024-09-12-at-11.36.48%E2%80%AFPM-1200x901.png)](https://themacweekly.com/83177/arts/keepin-it-weezy-voyage-to-the-blue-planet-tour-review/#photo)

Weezer on Xcel Center stage.

Honestly, they don’t look like much: four middle-aged white dudes brandishing sticker-adorned guitars and glasses, with only slight smiles suggesting any form of excitement (despite arriving on the stage via prop spaceship). With no backup dancers, no jumping around on stage, no crowd surfing or mosh pit – they still managed to pack the stadium to its very brim, nostalgia palpable as the audience screams. Standing still with no choreography or fanservice, Weezer began to play – nay, _shred_ – much to fans’ delight. These unassuming nerds are guys you’d probably pass any other day on the street, and they’re putting on a hell of a show.

This is the dichotomy of the rock band Weezer, caught between a memed-to-death “losercore” reputation and critically acclaimed widespread appeal across multiple generations. On our way to the Xcel Center — Weezer’s venue of choice for kicking off their “Voyage to the Blue Planet” tour on Sept. 4 — the cross-generational draw of the band became staggeringly apparent. Lining the streets and the halls of the stadium were millennials holding craft IPAs and matching their flannels to their “Blue Album” shirts, Gen Xers groaning about concession prices with their apathetic teenage children and Gen Z nerds – ourselves included – in Converse, Hot Topic cargo pants and thrifted oversized button- downs, stepping into the concert with a knowing self-awareness for the band’s reputation.

The reactions we got telling people about our plans for the evening ranged from judgmental eyebrow raises and laughter to sincere jealousy. To us, Weezer stands in a gray area of pop culture, with its fans expressing both tongue-in-cheek support and genuine love for the band.

To be fair, the dorky reputation the band has garnered is not without reason: the concert had its own (somewhat ridiculous) plot, a space drama (maybe, we hypothesized, inspired by the lead singer Rivers Cuomo’s own idea for a space-themed rock opera he had in the 90s!) complete with corny cutscenes about needing to “save the blue planet” by playing the entirety of the “Blue Album.” According to the show’s overarching story, Rivers Cuomo is an alien and so are all of us in the audience: the Weezeroids.

But this loose plot was nothing compared to the driving force of the music. The openers The Flaming Lips and Dinosaur Jr first brought energy into the crowd, but Weezer seemed to take it to another level. They started with some hits from their other albums – familiar radio-friendly numbers like “Island in the Sun,” “Beverly Hills” and “Pork and Beans.” After this, much to our surprise (and extreme joy), they moved on to songs from their second album “Pinkerton,” a cult favorite among fans, with a whopping four songs in a row: “Pink Triangle,” “Getchoo,” “Why Bother” and “Across the Sea”. Considering how many of the songs they played have been a public source of shame for Cuomo with their angsty and somewhat juvenile lyrics from his college days, it was a real treat to hear them live.

After these “classics,” they moved to start playing all of the “Blue Album,” kicking the songs off by claiming “the blue planet” as their own, as “one small step for Weezer, one giant leap for Weezerkind!” Here, the audience’s energy multiplied, with recognizable tunes like “Buddy Holly,” “Say It Ain’t So” and “Undone: The Sweater Song” hyping up old and new fans alike. And, in true Weezer fashion, there was no encore nor particularly flashy goodbye: only all six-plus minutes of “Only in Dreams” and a quick, humble thank you and farewell.

But, throughout the concert, we were mostly surprised by how much we knew by heart: even some of the more “deep cuts” had us dancing and singing in our seats just as much as the hits. Although we had found Weezer in different ways – with one of us growing up listening to Weezer in her dad’s car and one of us doing a discography deep-dive during the COVID-19 pandemic – we both shared with each other our fond memories associated with the band, phases in our lives where one specific song was our particular favorite, and the most out-of-pocket lyrics we’ve grown to laugh at and even relate to. It may sometimes be embarrassing to find Cuomo’s words relatable, but it is this very tension that makes being a Weezer fan worthwhile; the fanbase shares and revels in this awkwardness.

All this is to say that there is no one stereotype of a Weezer fan. Sure, it can be hard to overlook the TikTok jokes about it being “incel music,” the iconic “Buddy Holly” riff and (to be fair) the music they’ve released that’s pure garbage (“Raditude,” no matter how ironically you spin it, is an objectively horrible collection of music). But behind that façade of irony lies a band with a dedication to their music, a full embracement of their past rarely seen by other artists, and a deeply passionate fandom from all walks of life. As we listened to the music, sandwiched next to a Millennial couple and a Gen X skater, it became clear Weezer has something for everyone of all ages.

So, although that mosh pit was the stillest one we had ever seen, the overwhelming love radiating from every seat in that stadium made clear the impact of Weezer’s music on us all. Through all the canned dialogue and guitar solos, Weezer managed to unite thousands of people in the stadium and millions around the world, with authenticity and heartfelt energy.

[![Image 1](https://shipsofhagoth.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/WEEZER-VOYAGE-TO-BLUE-PHOTO-1-1024x614.jpg)](https://shipsofhagoth.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/WEEZER-VOYAGE-TO-BLUE-PHOTO-1.jpg)

In the immediate aftermath of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, every musical act in America cancelled their concerts for self-explanatory reasons. If I recall correctly, the very first band to resume touring and performing that fateful Fall was Weezer–presumably not out of any sense of defiance or protest or whatever, but simply because the band had bills to pay, and they and their fans needed to get out of their heads for an evening. I wondered if the band might make oblique allusion to that little factoid as I entered New York’s Madison Square Garden on September 11, 2024, to see Weezer launch their _Voyage to the Blue Planet_ tour.

Spoiler alert: they did not reference 9/11, and that was probably for the best. Weezer is very much a walking, talking Peter Pan-syndrome of a band, one trapped in a permanent state of arrested development, no matter how close they get to joining the AARP set; you do not check out latter-day Weezer to see how much they’ve grown or matured, but to make believe with them that you are still young as well, back when all your anxieties were strictly of the adolescent variety. Acknowledging 9/11–whether the original or the anniversary over 20 years later–would preclude that fantasy.

Not that I was terribly interested in that fantasy anymore. I have written [before](https://shipsofhagoth.com/2022/05/confessions-of-an-ex-weezer-fan/) about how, back in high school (right around the turn of the millennium and 9/11 as well, incidentally), I considered myself a die-hard Weezer fan. I had just about memorized their triple-platinum Blue album, and reverenced _Pinkerton_ as perhaps the most brutally-honest assessment of an awkward young man’s libido ever committed to CD. Sure, their comeback Green album and its immediate follow-up _Maladroit_ had been underwhelming, but we convinced ourselves that they were just shaking off the cobwebs and getting their mojo back, and would surely get back into top form in no time.

It wasn’t until I started BYU after my mission that Weezer finally dropped their fifth album _Make Believe_ in 2005, which was when my long-suffering fandom finally reached its limit. Oh I tried, I sincerely tried, to like it for old time’s sake! I tried to read “Beverly Hills” as some sort of cheekily-subversive parody of our celebrity-worshiping culture, rather than a dispiritingly-obvious symptom of it; I tried to sing-along to “Perfect Situation” without cringing; I tried to treat “We Are All On Drugs” as an _intentional_ joke.  All for naught! Here at last I could make no more excuses for them, the last of my ’90s-era goodwill was officially burned away, I was forced to confess: these songs were just plain _awful_. They had shifted from singing as teenagers to singing _as though_ they were teenagers, and the difference was immense and catastrophic. Their Peter Pan-syndrome and abject refusal to grow up had finally become a fatal liability.

Indeed, as I explained to a friend who came with me that night, part of why I had never bothered to see Weezer live all these years was that I simply didn’t want to pay money to sit through “Beverly Hills” and all their other post-Y2K dreck, on the off-chance I might hear a couple tracks off Blue or _Pinkerton_. No, Weezer and I had broken up in college, and we were never, ever getting back together. They were now just someone I used to know.

But as you get older, the siren call of nostalgia gets harder and harder to ignore, and the temptation to relive your youth, if only for an evening, becomes more and more seductive; hence, when Weezer announced that they would be playing the entirety of the the Blue album on its 30th anniversary, I decided it was high-time I pay my respects to not only my once-favorite-band but also my own dearly-departed youth, so I shelled out for a pair of tickets from those extortionists at Ticketmaster.

Fortunately the opening acts alone were almost worth the price of admission—indeed, they seemed almost too big to be mere opening acts themselves. Alt-Rock legends Dinosaur Jr. ripped through the hits in their 30-minute opening set, as J. Mascis stood their stolidly like the old, stoner hippie he’s always been, all while absolutely shredding one face-melting guitar solo after another. Recently-reunited bassist Lou Barlow, meanwhile, jumped around on stage with more personality than all of Weezer would exhibit later that evening. In a more just world, the reunion of the original Dinosaur Jr. lineup would be headlining MSG themselves. Highlights for me included their peon to friendship “[Freak Scene](https://m.youtube.com/watch?time_continue=4&v=5eO6up9Gpv0&embeds_referring_euri=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.google.com%2F&source_ve_path=MjM4NTE),” their biggest hit “[Feel The Pain](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=JXkN3nJyWEA&pp=ygUZZmVlbCB0aGUgcGFpbiBkaW5vc2F1ciBqcg%3D%3D),” and their Robert Smith-approved cover of “[Just Like Heaven](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=FJLOr8S2d2E&pp=ygUcanVzdCBsaWtlIGhlYXZlbiBkaW5vc2F1ciBqcg%3D%3D).”

Second opener The Flaming Lips had even more personality than both bands combined: Wayne Coyne worked the crowd like a magician for their 50-minute set, he had even non-fans singing along to their earliest hit “[She Don’t Use Jelly](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=cvfxKbpoxRE&pp=ygUgZmxhbWluZyBsaXBzIHNoZSBkb24ndCB1c2UgamVsbHk%3D),” they inflated a pair of 20-foot pink robots on stage for “[Yoshimi Battles The Pink Robots](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=AzlMeTxVdH8&pp=ygUsZmxhbWluZyBsaXBzIHlvc2hpbWkgYmF0dGxlcyB0aGUgcGluayByb2JvdHM%3D)” (natch), and of course they saved their biggest hit “[Do You Realize??](https://shipsofhagoth.com/2024/02/do-you-realize-by-the-flaming-lips-annotated-readings/)” for the grand finale, which Coyne sang under an inflatable rainbow. No crowd-surfing inside a giant gerbil ball like he became famous for in the 2000s, but I can respect that 1) he might be tired of that gimmick by now, and 2) he’s not gonna risk his personal safety for an opening act. Yet The Lips were also the one opener that clearly had fans present to see _them_, not the headliner.

[![Image 2](https://shipsofhagoth.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/IMG_3324-2-768x1024.jpeg)](https://shipsofhagoth.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/IMG_3324-2-scaled.jpeg)

Nevertheless, the vast majority of attendees at MSG that night were there for one reason and one reason only: to see Weezer perform the Blue album in its entirety. The original CD clocks in at a quite reasonable 41 minutes, so I thought there was a decent chance that Weezer might respect the fact that most of their fans are now pushing middle-age and had work in the morning.

Alas, when Weezer finally took the stage, the opening notes were not the familiar finger-picking of “My Name Is Jonas,” but of the “Futurescope trilogy” that closes out 2014’s _Everything Will Be Alright In The End_ (the only other time since _Make Believe_ I let myself get fooled into giving a new Weezer album a chance). I whipped out my phone and quickly found their set-list from the night previous, where my worst fears were confirmed: they would be performing a dozen or so songs from the 21st century, followed by a half-dozen _Pinkerton_ tracks, before they finally, _finally_ launched into the Blue album. I would not be getting home at a decent hour after all. My friend busted-up laughing when he saw “Beverly Hills” on the set-list. “Foiled again!” I exclaimed.

(I also had to wonder why, if they were going to include any tracks at all from _Everything Will Be Alright In The End_, Weezer didn’t go with “[Back To The Shack](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3H89GXU9OeU)“–ya know, the one where he explicitly sings “Rocking out like it’s ’94.” It would’ve been pandering, yes, but then the whole show was pandering; they might as well have just leaned into it.)

The band had to have known that the whole reason they were selling-out Madison Square Gardens for the first time in years (possibly ever) was because everyone just wanted to hear the ‘90s stuff again. Heck, I remember when they had done a similar Blue-and-_Pinkerton_\-only tour a dozen or so years earlier; as more than one online-rag noted at the time, even Weezer knew no one wants to hear their newer crap. (The reason I didn’t go see them then was because you had to buy a second ticket to hear the _Pinkerton_\-only concert on the same tour, which price-gouging of their oldest fans didn’t sit right with me; that and I was still a broke-ass grad student). This wasn’t a blind spot for the band, they’ve known full well for years what their fans actually want. Yet still they barreled ahead with their 2000s oeuvre, even though avoiding the same was the whole selling point of this tour in the first place.

Hence, I couldn’t help but wonder if Cuomo, as he’s gotten on in years himself and started to worry about his long-term legacy, was here trying to make the case that his post-Y2k output should be treated with the same respect and reverence as his ’90s work. Listen to how awesome “Island In The Sun” sounds at concert-venue decibels, he seemed to say! Hear how similar “Pork and Beans” is to _Pinkerton_, kinda! Surely “Beverly Hills” is as iconic as “[Buddy Holly](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=kemivUKb4f4)” by now, right? Aren’t you as moved by “Any Friend of Diane’s” as by the bridge to “[Say It Ain’t So](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=ENXvZ9YRjbo)”? Isn’t the time I wrote “Hash Pipe” and “Dope Nose” the same day as famous as the time Dolly Parton did the same with “Jolene” and “I Will Always Love You”? Oh, and “Perfect Situation” is just as fun to sing along to as “[The Sweater Song](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LHQqqM5sr7g)”, I swear!

Such all seemed to be his argument, anyways; nevertheless, the moment Weezer launched into “[Getchoo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_8ESeMaT1jc)” for the _Pinkerton_ portion of the show, the difference in quality between their pre- and post-2000 songs was stark and undeniable. The band didn’t even play the best tracks off _Pinkerton_ (i.e. “[El Scorcho](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=okthJIVbi6g),” “[The Good Life](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gkroIXktjgE),” and “[Falling For You](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hdrAsZ7ebuc)“); but even the lesser-tracks they _did_ deign to play (why on God’s green earth would you still sing “Across the Sea” in the Year of Our Lord 2024?!) were heads-and-shoulders better than everything that preceded it. It was like switching from margarine to Irish Butter, from black-and-white to technicolor, from analog to HD, from Sunkist to Simply Orange, from Walmart house-brand soda to a real Dr Pepper. If Cuomo was making a case for his latter-day output, he failed; but if his goal in playing these mediocrities was to get me even more pumped up for the _actual_ good stuff, he succeeded masterfully.

[![Image 3](https://shipsofhagoth.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/IMG_3331-6-1024x770.jpeg)](https://shipsofhagoth.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/IMG_3331-6-scaled.jpeg)

And indeed, when the opening power-chords of “[My Name Is Jonas](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qsXmTBTcHz8)” at last rang out through the loud-speakers, the crowd went wild and I with it. In an instant, I was swept right back to my teen years, almost in spite of myself. Was it all just a blatant and commercialized nostalgia trip? Dear reader, I. Did. Not. Care! I gladly succumbed. For once, their Peter Pan syndrome was an asset rather than a liability. For the following 40-odd minutes I belted out, with thousands of my closest friends, every word to an album I’d had memorized since high school, without hypocrisy and without guile.

It was an album I had long ago overplayed and lost all ability to listen to freshly; but for that one night only, I was able to hear it as though it were new again. Suddenly it was like the intervening quarter-century—9/11, the invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan, wars and rumors of wars, global warming, global pandemics, global inflation, global resurgences in white-supremacism, nationalism, and authoritarianism, not to mention jobs and careers, bills, bed-times, student loans, kids to raise, retirement accounts, wrinkles, graying hairs, and a thousand other things major and minor besides—had never happened, for all is as only one day unto God, and time is measured only unto man. Was this a cowardly abnegation of responsibility on my part, or a strategic withdrawal to reflect and recharge, like Christ in the wilderness? Judge not, lest ye be judged.

The band thankfully kept the stage banter to a minimum throughout their 2-hour set; the theme of their multi-media stage-show was literally “Voyage to a Blue Planet,” performing as though they were astronauts traveling to a distant blue planet “30 light years away”, passing through such obstacles as the Pinkerton asteroid belt and such. The “twist” towards the end was when Rivers Cuomo revealed that he was a native of the Blue planet all along. “I’m an alien,” he told the crowd in his performatively-awkward way, “And so are you!”

Though the bit was cheesy, he was inadvertently teaching true doctrine: we are all indeed “strangers and pilgrims” on the earth. If we recurrently feel ourselves unable to reconcile ourselves to the unrelenting horrors and injustices of this world—every terrorist attack, every “ethnic cleansing,” every oppression, repression, mass deportation, hate crime, act of bigotry, ignorance, violence, and/or senseless cruelty—no matter how long we live here, it’s because we accurately intuit that we don’t actually belong here at all. As GK Chesterton, CS Lewis, and even Hugh Nibley have all preached before, we all feel that we belong elsewhere, that we in fact _came_ from elsewhere, somewhere celestial—the same place we’re intended to return _to_. Indeed, we’re supposed to live as though we were back there already right _now_: “[Surf Wax America](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mM2tt0Mc-1w)‘s” rousing chorus of “You take your car to work, I’ll take my board/And when you’re out of fuel, I’m still float” rings as true today—as a clarion call to reject the vanities of this world and seek for the things of a better—as it did in 1994.

My eyes were closed almost the entire time they tore through the Blue album, truth be told—partly cause I was head-banging so hard; partly cause there frankly wasn’t much to see as the band just stood there stiffly in front of their microphones the whole time; partly cause their space-themed stage-set was kinda cringe; partly cause seeing how old these guys in their 50s now look would kinda break the spell—but also partly cause I didn’t _need_ to see them. For I could hear them, I could _feel_ them, I could experience them, like the Holy Spirit itself, which whispereth through and pierceth all things, and often times it maketh my bones to quake while it maketh manifest—

How a Trip to the Grocery Store Helped Weezer Make the Blue Album
=================================================================

[Corey Irwin](https://loudwire.com/author/coreyirwin/)

[Corey Irwin](https://loudwire.com/author/coreyirwin/)Updated: April 13, 2024

Gary Livingston/Newsmakers, Getty Images / Geffen

*   [SHARE](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=http%3A%2F%2Floudwire.com%2Fweezer-grocery-store-blue-album%2F%3Ftrackback%3Dfbshare_mobile "SHARE")
*   [TWEET](http://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=How%20a%20Trip%20to%20the%20Grocery%20Store%20Helped%20Weezer%20Make%20the%20Blue%20Album%20http%3A%2F%2Floudwire.com%2Fweezer-grocery-store-blue-album%2F%3Ftrackback%3Dtwitter_mobile%20%40Loudwire "TWEET")

[Rivers Cuomo](https://loudwire.com/tags/rivers-cuomo/) has revealed how a simple trip to the grocery store helped [Weezer](https://loudwire.com/tags/weezer/) create their 1994 self-titled debut, commonly referred to as the Blue Album.

In hindsight, it’s easy to see why the LP was a success. The Blue Album is chock full of such modern classics as “Buddy Holly,” “Say It Ain’t So” and “Undone (The Sweater Song).” Still, Weezer was an unknown band at the time, and there was no guarantee that anyone would pay attention to them.

After signing their record deal, the band wanted to self-produce their debut album. However, the label wasn’t comfortable giving a new act such power.

“We got a record deal with Geffen and we thought we knew exactly how we wanted the record to sound. We don’t want a producer,” Cuomo recalled during a recent interview with [Booker & Stryker](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bMIUcSNmITA). “But \[the label\] absolutely insisted. ‘This is your first album. Second album, we can talk about, but first album you guys need a producer.’”

**READ MORE:** **[The 35 Best Mustaches in Rock Music](https://loudwire.com/best-mustaches-rock-metal/)**

Unsure of who to work with, Cuomo pondered over the decision. Then, during an innocuous visit to his local supermarket, the frontman had an epiphany.

“One day I was in the grocery store picking up some ramen noodles or whatever. And on the Muzak in there comes the [Cars](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/the-cars/) song, ‘Just What I Needed.’”

Cuomo was struck by the tune’s guitar punch, coupled with its instantly-recognizable keyboard line.

“And I was like, ‘Man, that’s exactly what we want to sound like! So let’s get that guy!’”

### Ric Ocasek Was 'Blown Away' by Weezer's Tunes

Fatefully, “that guy” turned out to be the Cars’ frontman and songwriter, [Ric Ocasek](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/tags/ric-ocasek/), rather than Roy Thomas Baker, who actually produced “Just What I Needed.” Cuomo reached out to Ocasek directly, and was excited by the response.

“We sent him our demo tape and he immediately responded and was totally blown away and very enthusiastic,” the singer recalled. “Whereas most of the people in the industry so far, we’d given them our tape and they were like, ‘Eh.’ But he really got it, so we went with him.”

With Ocasek’s guidance, Weezer found the sound they were looking for. The Blue Album became one of the defining albums of the ‘90s, selling more than 15 million copies worldwide. Weeezer will celebrate the LP’s 30th anniversary by embarking on a nationwide tour dubbed [Voyage to the Blue Planet](https://ultimateclassicrock.com/weezer-voyage-to-the-blue-planet-tour/). It will see the band performing the Blue Album in its entirety, along with further hits from throughout their career.

[Weezer](https://consequence.net/artist/weezer/) have announced a concert film shot during their [ongoing 2024 tour](https://consequence.net/2024/03/weezer-blue-album-30th-anniversary-tour/) (get tickets [here](https://stubhub.prf.hn/click/camref:1100l9Pt3/pubref:weezer*blue-album-concert-film/destination:https%3A%2F%2Fwww.stubhub.com%2Fweezer-tickets%2Fperformer%2F389)) celebrating the 30th anniversary of their self-titled debut, aka _The Blue Album_.

Titled _Weezer’s Voyage to the Blue Planet: The Concert Film_, it was captured at Boston’s TD Garden on September 10th and will livestream at [Moment.co](https://www.moment.co/weezer) on October 13th and 14th.

[Get Weezer Tickets Here](https://stubhub.prf.hn/click/camref:1100l9Pt3/pubref:weezer*blue-album-concert-film-button/destination:https%3A%2F%2Fwww.stubhub.com%2Fweezer-tickets%2Fperformer%2F389)

$13 early bird tickets will be available through September 27th at noon Pacific Time, after which the price will rise to $16. Tickets purchased the day of will be available for $18. A replay of the film will be up for 24 hours after it streams. Tickets are available [here](https://www.moment.co/weezer).

Related Video

Weezer are also celebrating the _Blue Album_’s 30th anniversary with an [expansive reissue](https://consequence.net/2024/09/weezer-the-blue-album-30th-anniversary-edition/) featuring 36 unreleased tracks. [Pre-orders](https://amzn.to/47EYeff) are ongoing ahead of its release on November 1st.

Featuring special guests Flaming Lips and Dinosaur Jr., Weezer’s tour has remaining dates throughout Texas, the Pacific Northwest, and California. See the full schedule below, and [pick up tickets here](https://stubhub.prf.hn/click/camref:1100l9Pt3/pubref:weezer*blue-album-concert-film/destination:https%3A%2F%2Fwww.stubhub.com%2Fweezer-tickets%2Fperformer%2F389).
